title: Al-Ghashiyah: the overwhelming
hookLine: faces that day humbled, and faces that day joyful (88:1–16)

lines: THE NEWS IS IN THE FACE.
cards: A face gives the news before the mouth does. The doctor coming through the double doors. The teacher handing back the exam.
A friend across the table who hasn't said a word yet. The story is already there, in the eyes and the set of the jaw. The surah before Al-Fajr tells the story of the Day through faces.
Not scales or books, this time. Two kinds of faces, set side by side, and a question underneath simple enough to carry all day. Today: Al-Ghashiyah, the overwhelming.

teach.b: Surah eighty-eight opens with a question, in Pickthall's words: Hath there come unto thee tidings of the Overwhelming?
Al-ghashiyah comes from a root meaning to cover, to wrap completely, the way a wave covers a swimmer or a faint covers your senses.
Commentators take it as a name for the Day of Judgment: the event that covers everything, that nobody can stand outside of.
Then the faces. Some, that day, humbled, toiling, worn out; their work was hard and brought them nowhere. Others, that day, joyful, na'imah, soft with ease.
And the next phrase is the surprise: pleased with their effort. The word for effort is sa'y, the same word met in Al-Layl ten days ago: your strivings differ.
Both groups worked. Some commentators draw the lesson plainly: the difference wasn't effort; it was where the effort went, and what it was for.
The joyful faces are placed in a lofty garden, with flowing springs, raised couches, cups set out, cushions lined up, carpets spread, like a host who has prepared everything before the guest arrives.

A hadith in Muslim's collection says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited it, together with Al-A'la, in the Friday prayer and the Eid prayers. So it's a surah often heard in a crowd, on a festival morning, surrounded by faces.

how: Following the Prophet's practice, imams often recite Al-Ghashiyah, with Al-A'la, in the Friday prayer and the prayers of the two Eids, so it is a surah often heard in congregation.

o: the Overwhelming, a name for the Day that covers all
the joyful faces in the garden on that day
a well in the desert where caravans stop to drink

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.

s: in Al-Ghashiyah only the joyful faces worked hard
both worked; the humbled faces toiled too. the difference is where the effort went.
the Prophet recited Al-Ghashiyah in the Friday and Eid prayers
a hadith in Muslim's collection pairs it with Al-A'la.
al-ghashiyah comes from a root meaning to cover
the Day that covers everything, like a wave over a swimmer.

games.q: Al-Ghashiyah says some faces that day will be joyful. what does it say they are pleased with?
games.why: pleased with their effort, li-sa'yiha (88:9): the same sa'y as Al-Layl. effort pointed well is what the joy looks back on.

practice: Notice your own face, the forehead, the jaw, the space between your eyebrows, and let anything clenched soften.
Then think of one piece of work you're doing now, and picture looking back on it one day, your face open, pleased with the effort. What would have to be true of that work?

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghashiyah. The overwhelming, the Day that covers everything, and the name of Surah eighty-eight, told in faces. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the overwhelming, from gh-sh-y, to cover completely; a name for the Day of Judgment.

carryVoice: Your line: which face. Both faces worked; only one is pleased with it. One more day to two hundred.

sources.q: Hath there come unto thee tidings of the Overwhelming?

sources.ref: Qur'an 88:2–16 (the two kinds of faces; the garden)
